verdict.rationale: The canon supplies one stable lexical pattern of a once-given, sufficient, sealed deposit. Hebrews 1:1-2 sets prior prophetic speech (the aorist participle, a completed past action in participle form, 'having spoken' (λαλήσας) with 'of old' (πάλαι), plus 'in many parts' (πολυμερῶς) and 'in many ways' (πολυτρόπως)) against terminal Son-speech 'in these last days, in a Son' (ἐπ’ ἐσχάτου τῶν ἡμερῶν τούτων ἐν υἱῷ). Ephesians 2:20 builds the church on a finished foundation (the aorist passive participle, a completed past action in participle form done to the subject, 'having been built upon' (ἐποικοδομηθέντες)) with Christ as 'cornerstone' (ἀκρογωνιαῖος, only 2 New Testament occurrences). Jude 3 marks the faith 'once for all delivered' (ἅπαξ παραδοθείσῃ), the adverb modifying an aorist passive participle (completed past action in participle form done to the subject). Second Timothy 3:16-17 calls 'all Scripture God-breathed' (πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος, theopneustos being a New Testament hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire New Testament)) sufficient 'so that complete might be' (ἵνα ἄρτιος ᾖ, artios also a New Testament hapax (a word occurring only once in the entire New Testament)) the man of God. Galatians 1:8-9 attaches 'curse' (ἀνάθεμα) to any 'contrary to which' (παρ’ ὃ) gospel, and Revelation 22:18-19 applies the add, subtract formula ('add to' (ἐπιτίθημι), 'take away' (ἀφαιρέω)) that reproduces Deuteronomy 4:2 and Proverbs 30:6. The one real lexical seam is that 'once' (ἅπαξ) also carries a bare numerical sense in this same corpus, but the parallel in Jude 5 and the participle favor the definitive 'once for all' sense here.

scripture.reasoning: 'In many parts and in many ways of old God spoke to the fathers in the prophets' (Πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως πάλαι ὁ θεὸς λαλήσας τοῖς πατράσιν ἐν τοῖς προφήταις). MorphGNT (the morphologically tagged Greek New Testament) tags 'having spoken' (λαλήσας) as an aorist active participle (a completed past action in participle form, active voice; tag V- -AAPNSM-), and with 'of old' (πάλαι) it positions prophetic speech as a completed past mode, lexically bounded and partial. The paired adverbs 'in many parts' (πολυμερῶς) and 'in many ways' (πολυτρόπως) form a two-term scope figure that delimits the prior prophetic mode as fragmentary against the Son-speech of verse 2.

'In these last days he spoke to us in a Son' (ἐπ’ ἐσχάτου τῶν ἡμερῶν τούτων ἐλάλησεν ἡμῖν ἐν υἱῷ). The main verb 'he spoke' (ἐλάλησεν) is aorist indicative (a completed past action stated as straightforward fact; tag 3AAI-S--); the locative phrase 'in these last days' (ἐπ’ ἐσχάτου τῶν ἡμερῶν τούτων) is eschatologically terminal (pointing to the final epoch of history), and the contrast 'in the prophets' (ἐν τοῖς προφήταις) versus 'in a Son' (ἐν υἱῷ) frames Son-speech as the final mode and the heir 'heir' (κληρονόμον) as the consummating addressee, lexically closing the prophetic series.

'Having been built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone' (ἐποικοδομηθέντες ἐπὶ τῷ θεμελίῳ τῶν ἀποστόλων καὶ προφητῶν, ὄντος ἀκρογωνιαίου αὐτοῦ Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ). MorphGNT (the morphologically tagged Greek New Testament) tags 'having been built upon' (ἐποικοδομηθέντες) as an aorist passive participle (a completed past action in participle form done to the subject; tag V- -APPNPM-), presenting the church as already built upon a fixed 'foundation' (θεμελίῳ). 'cornerstone' (ἀκρογωνιαῖος) occurs only twice in the New Testament, here and 1 Peter 2:6 (queried count 2), a one-laid-once architectural metaphor incompatible with ongoing foundational revelation.

'For the faith once delivered to the saints' (τῇ ἅπαξ παραδοθείσῃ τοῖς ἁγίοις πίστει). MorphGNT (the morphologically tagged Greek New Testament) tags 'once' (ἅπαξ) as an indeclinable adverb (an adverb whose form never changes; tag D-) and 'having been delivered' (παραδοθείσῃ) as an aorist passive participle (a completed past action in participle form done to the subject; tag V- -APPDSF-), so 'once' (ἅπαξ) modifies a completed delivery, marking the faith as once delivered. The infinitive 'to contend for' (ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι) presupposes a finished, identifiable deposit. The same author uses 'once' (ἅπαξ) two verses later (Jude 5, 'knowing once for all all things' (εἰδότας ἅπαξ πάντα)) in the definitive 'once for all' sense, which supports that sense here, though 'once' (ἅπαξ) elsewhere in the corpus can mean a bare numerical 'once'.

'If anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues written in this book' (ἐάν τις ἐπιθῇ ἐπ’ αὐτά, ἐπιθήσει ὁ θεὸς ἐπ’ αὐτὸν τὰς πληγὰς τὰς γεγραμμένας ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τούτῳ). The verb 'add to' (ἐπιτίθημι, in the aorist subjunctive form 'might add' (ἐπιθῇ), and the future form 'will add' (ἐπιθήσει)) is used with talionic word-play (a 'measure-for-measure' rhetorical move where the same act done by the offender returns on him); 'having been written' (γεγραμμένας) is a perfect passive participle (a completed past action whose result still stands in participle form done to the subject; tag V- -XPPAPF-) that treats the text as already-written and fixed. The immediate referent is this 'book' (βιβλίον), but the lexical formula reproduces Deuteronomy 4:2 (queried: do not add, do not take away) and functions as a sealed-deposit motif.

'If anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy' (ἐάν τις ἀφέλῃ ἀπὸ τῶν λόγων τοῦ βιβλίου τῆς προφητείας ταύτης). 'take away' (ἀφαιρέω, in subtract sense, aorist subjunctive 'might take away' (ἀφέλῃ), future 'will take away' (ἀφελεῖ)) paired with 'add to' (ἐπιτίθημι) in verse 18 yields a closed-text formula; 'having been written' (γεγραμμένων) is again a perfect passive participle (a completed past action whose result still stands in participle form done to the subject; tag V- -XPPGPM-). The chain 'of the words of the book of the prophecy' (τῶν λόγων τοῦ βιβλίου τῆς προφητείας, a chain of nouns in the 'of-X, of-Y, of-Z' possessive form called the genitive) identifies the deposit as prophetic word-content sealed against additive or subtractive revision, matching the Hebrew add, subtract pair in Deuteronomy 4:2 and Deuteronomy 13:1.

'And if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed' (καὶ ἐὰν ἡμεῖς ἢ ἄγγελος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ εὐαγγελίζηται ὑμῖν παρ’ ὃ εὐηγγελισάμεθα ὑμῖν, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω). MorphGNT (the morphologically tagged Greek New Testament) shows 'beside, contrary to' (παρά) governing the accusative (the 'direct-object' grammatical form) relative 'which' (ὃ), marking deviation from the delivered 'gospel' (εὐαγγέλιον); the 'if-then' clause (a conditional, an 'if-then' clause) includes even an apostle ('we' (ἡμεῖς)) or an angel, lexically excluding any subsequent revelatory authority that supplements or alters the apostolic message. 'curse' (ἀνάθεμα) occurs only 6 times in the New Testament (queried), always negative.

'If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed' (εἴ τις ὑμᾶς εὐαγγελίζεται παρ’ ὃ παρελάβετε, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω). The second iteration intensifies the prior 'if-then' clause (the prior conditional, an 'if-then' clause); 'receive by tradition' (παραλαμβάνω, aorist 'you received' (παρελάβετε), receive by tradition) ties the standard to what the Galatians already received, treating the apostolic deposit as the lexical norm against which all later proclamation is measured.

'All Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness' (πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος καὶ ὠφέλιμος πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, πρὸς ἐλεγμόν, πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν, πρὸς παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ). MorphGNT (the morphologically tagged Greek New Testament) tags 'God-breathed' (θεόπνευστος) as a predicate adjective (an adjective completing a 'X is Y' statement; tag A- ----NSF-) of 'Scripture' (γραφή); queried occurrence count is 1, a New Testament hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire New Testament), so it locates inspiration as an intrinsic property of 'Scripture' (γραφή). The fourfold 'for' (πρός) series (teaching, reproof, correction, training) covers the categories of the rule of faith (the settled core of Christian belief used as a standard).

'So that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work' (ἵνα ἄρτιος ᾖ ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος, πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτισμένος). The result clause 'so that complete might be' (ἵνα ἄρτιος ᾖ) uses 'complete' (ἄρτιος, queried count 1, New Testament hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire New Testament)) plus the perfect passive participle 'having been completely equipped' (ἐξηρτισμένος, a completed past action whose result still stands in participle form done to the subject; tag V- -XPPNSM-, lemma ἐξαρτίζω, completely equipped) to assert sufficiency of 'Scripture' (γραφή) for every good work, lexically marking no additional revelatory supplement as necessary for the stated purpose.

complicating_texts.resolution: The immediate lexical referent of 'book' (βιβλίον) is the Apocalypse itself (the book of Revelation), not the whole canon, and the noun 'book' (βιβλίον) occurs 35 times across the New Testament (queried) with no inherent whole-canon sense. So this text does not by itself close the canon. Its force in the verdict is that it applies the Deuteronomy 4:2 and Proverbs 30:6 add, subtract formula (verified in the Hebrew text and corroborated by 51 and 41 OpenBible votes) to a written prophetic deposit, and is cumulative with Jude 3, Galatians 1:8-9, and 2 Timothy 3:16-17, not solitary.

Jude 5 uses the same adverb 'once' (ἅπαξ, Strong's G0530) as Jude 3, in the clause 'knowing once for all all things' (εἰδότας ἅπαξ πάντα). This is a complicating data point because 'once' (ἅπαξ) across its 14 canon occurrences carries two senses: a bare numerical 'once' (1 Thessalonians 2:18, 2 Corinthians 11:25, Philippians 4:16, Hebrews 9:7) and a definitive 'once for all' (1 Peter 3:18, Hebrews 9:26-28, Hebrews 6:4). The Jude 5 parallel resolves the ambiguity toward the definitive sense in Jude 3, since the same author in adjacent context uses it of a settled, complete knowledge, not a countable single act.

Paul writes that 'prophecies will be done away' (προφητεῖαι καταργηθήσονται) and 'knowledge will be done away' (γνῶσις καταργηθήσεται) when 'the perfect' (τὸ τέλειον) arrives. The verbs are future passive of 'be done away' (καταργέω), so the text marks prophetic and knowledge gifts as terminable in their constitutive function rather than perpetual. The exegetical debate over 'the perfect' (τὸ τέλειον, possible senses: maturity, the second coming, the completed deposit) is downstream of the lexical observation that the gifts are explicitly marked as ending.

Peter cites Joel, 'I will pour out from my Spirit and they will prophesy' (ἐκχεῶ ἀπὸ τοῦ πνεύματός μου καὶ προφητεύσουσιν), locating Spirit-outpouring prophecy 'in the last days' (ἐν ταῖς ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις), the same last-days epoch Hebrews 1:2 ties to the Son-revelation. The text affirms prophecy contemporaneous with the foundation-laying of Ephesians 2:20, not an open-ended additive canon, so it complicates a strong cessation reading (the view that miraculous gifts have ceased) but not the closure of the foundational deposit.

'Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh' (προφῆται δὲ δύο ἢ τρεῖς λαλείτωσαν, καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι διακρινέτωσαν). Assembly prophecy is subject to 'weighing' (διάκρισις), by other prophets, lexically marking such utterances as non-self-authenticating and measured against a discernible standard, which Galatians 1:8-9 identifies as the apostolic 'gospel' (εὐαγγέλιον). This shows ongoing prophetic speech existed but did not function as canon-grade revelation.

variants.note: None of the cited verses fall within the ingested ECM window (3 John 1:1 to 1:15, where ECM means 'the critical edition of New Testament textual variants'), so this is not_in_ecm_scope; the bundle returned zero variant units. The load-bearing lexical anchors ('God-breathed' (θεόπνευστος), 'once' (ἅπαξ), 'cornerstone' (ἀκρογωνιαῖος), 'curse' (ἀνάθεμα), 'add to' (ἐπιτίθημι), 'take away' (ἀφαιρέω), 'complete' (ἄρτιος)) were checked across the Nestle1904 and SBLGNT editions present in the lexical store and agree in lemma and form; no editorial variant disturbs the terms on which the verdict rests.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads Hebrews 1:1-2 as a completed arc from polymeric prophetic speech (the aorist participle, a completed past action in participle form, 'having spoken' (λαλήσας), 'of old' (πάλαι)) to terminal Son-speech, with Jude 3 'once' (ἅπαξ) taken in its definitive 'once for all' sense (supported by the Jude 5 parallel) and 2 Timothy 3:16-17 sufficiency ('God-breathed' (θεόπνευστος), 'complete' (ἄρτιος)) plus the Revelation 22, Deuteronomy 4:2 seal formula closing the deposit. On this reading the words foreclose any later revelation of equal rank.

Reads 'once' (ἅπαξ) in Jude 3 as plausibly the bare numerical 'once' attested elsewhere in the same corpus (1 Thessalonians 2:18, 2 Corinthians 11:25, Hebrews 9:7), and notes that the immediate referent of 'book' (βιβλίον) in Revelation 22:18-19 is the Apocalypse alone (the book of Revelation alone), that Ephesians 2:20 names prophets alongside apostles in the foundation, and that Acts 2:17-18 and 1 Corinthians 14:29-32 show prophecy continuing in the last-days church. On this reading the vocabulary affirms a unique apostolic deposit but does not by itself rule out later subordinate revelation, leaving the strict closure claim underdetermined by the words alone.

hermeneutics.notes: Verdict rests on the lexical force of 'once' (ἅπαξ), 'cornerstone' (ἀκρογωνιαῖος), 'God-breathed' (θεόπνευστος), 'complete' (ἄρτιος), and the talionic 'add to' (ἐπιτίθημι) and 'take away' (ἀφαιρέω) pair in Revelation 22:18-19 read against the Hebrew add, subtract formula of Deuteronomy 4:2, Deuteronomy 13:1, and Proverbs 30:6 (analogia scripturae, the principle that Scripture interprets Scripture), all verified in the lexical store. Hebrews 1:1-2 supplies the redemptive-historical framing: prior prophetic speech culminates 'in a Son' (ἐν υἱῷ) 'in these last days' (ἐπ’ ἐσχάτου τῶν ἡμερῶν τούτων). The cessationism (the view that miraculous gifts have ceased) versus continuationism (the view that miraculous gifts continue) frameworks bear only on whether subordinate prophecy continues, not on whether the foundational deposit is closed; the open-revelation lens is recorded fairly because 'once' (ἅπαξ) is genuinely two-sensed in this corpus.

stem_audit.notes: The stem, that no revelation given after the apostolic age stands on par with Scripture or adds to the rule of faith (the settled core of Christian belief used as a standard), is a descriptive closure claim and does not smuggle its own verdict; it leaves open whether the lexical pattern supports closure. The phrase rule of faith is a category term, not a tradition-specific taxonomy, and the proposition is testable against the words. No neutralization needed. The lexical evidence confirms the closure pattern, so affirms is retained from the prior file.

lay_summary: The biblical text uses specific Greek vocabulary that frames the apostolic-era deposit as a once-given, sufficient, and protected body of revelation. Hebrews 1:1-2 contrasts prior prophetic speech as in many parts (polymerōs) and in many ways (polytropōs), of old (palai), with the Son-speech of these last days, positioning the Son-revelation as the final mode of God speaking. Ephesians 2:20 describes the church as already built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone (akrogōniaios), a word used only twice in the New Testament, an image of a foundation laid once. Jude 3 calls believers to contend for the faith once delivered (hapax paradotheisē) to the saints, where the adverb 'once' (hapax) modifies a completed delivery. Second Timothy 3:16-17 says all Scripture (graphē) is God-breathed (theopneustos), a word found nowhere else in the New Testament, and sufficient so the person of God may be complete (artios), also a once-only word, and fully equipped for every good work. Galatians 1:8-9 attaches the curse 'anathema' twice to anyone, even an apostle or angel, who preaches a gospel contrary to what was received. Revelation 22:18-19 uses the add and take-away pair (epitithēmi and aphaireō) against changing the words of the book (biblion), the same formula found in Deuteronomy 4:2, Deuteronomy 13:1, and Proverbs 30:6, which were checked in the Hebrew text. Read together these texts give one consistent pattern of a sealed, sufficient deposit. Readers diverge for two text-level reasons that are honest to name. First, the word 'once' (hapax) in this same set of writings sometimes means simply once in number, as in 'once I was stoned', and sometimes means 'once for all', as of Christ suffering once for sins, so a careful reader can ask which sense Jude 3 carries, though the same author in the next sentences uses it in the settled sense. Second, the 'book' (biblion) in Revelation 22 most directly names that one book, not the whole collection, so its sealing force reaches the wider canon only through the repeated Old Testament formula, not by itself. The closure reading takes the definitive sense and the cumulative pattern; the open reading takes the numerical sense and the narrow referent and finds the strict claim underdetermined by the words alone.
